title: Dropout: Preventing Overfitting by Dropping Units
hook: Randomly delete units during each training step and you stop neurons from co-adapting - which is secretly like training a huge ensemble of thinned networks and averaging them at test time.
key_points: Randomly drops units and their connections during training, so neurons can't rely on specific co-adaptations.
Training effectively samples from an exponential number of 'thinned' sub-networks.
At test time, a single network with scaled-down weights approximates averaging all those sub-networks.
Reduced overfitting and improved results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology.
content_html: Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky and colleagues introduced dropout in their 2014 JMLR paper as a simple cure for overfitting in large neural networks. The idea is almost suspiciously cheap: during training, randomly switch off units so the network can never lean too hard on any single feature detector.
extra_html:
How it works

On each training step, dropout randomly removes units along with their connections, so a different "thinned" version of the network sees each batch. This prevents units from co-adapting too much - a neuron can't count on a specific partner always being present, so it has to learn features that are useful more broadly. Over training, this effectively samples from an exponential number of sub-networks. At test time you don't run all of them; instead a single network with weights scaled down to match the dropout rate approximates averaging the whole ensemble in one forward pass.

Why it matters

Treating dropout as cheap model averaging gave a principled story for why it works so well, and the authors showed it reduced overfitting and improved results across vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology. That breadth made it a default regularizer in deep learning for years.

related.title: Overfitting & Regularization
related.hook: A model that aces its training data but flops on anything new hasn't learned — it has memorized. Regularization is the cure.

related.title: Batch Normalization
related.hook: Re-center and re-scale each layer's activations on every minibatch, and deep nets suddenly train faster and tolerate much higher learning rates.

flashcards.prompt: Why does randomly dropping units during training reduce overfitting?
flashcards.back_html: It stops neurons from co-adapting — a unit can't rely on a specific partner always being present, so it learns features useful more broadly.

flashcards.prompt: What is the ensemble interpretation of dropout?

choices.text: Training samples from an exponential number of thinned sub-networks; testing approximates averaging them
It trains one network and discards the worst-performing neurons
It literally trains and stores thousands of separate models

flashcards.explanation_html: Each step sees a different thinned network; at test time, one network with scaled-down weights approximates averaging the ensemble.

flashcards.prompt: How is dropout handled at test time?

choices.text: A single network with weights scaled down to match the dropout rate, in one forward pass
All sub-networks are run and their outputs averaged
Dropout stays active to keep behavior consistent

flashcards.explanation_html: Rather than running every sub-network, a single net with scaled-down weights approximates the ensemble average in one pass.
